name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: If Wisconsin is in great financial shape, why can’t we afford to fund our schools?
text:
A hallway in La Follette High School in Madison. (Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)It was a dreary, rainy Thursday morning when the state education department announced some depressing news: According to the final, official numbers, 62% of Wisconsin school districts will receive less money in state general aid this year than they did last year. 
Schools are struggling because, for the third year in a row, the state budget put no new money into general school aid, the Department of Public Instruction pointed out in an Oct. 15 press release. That’s after more than 15 years during which per-pupil spending in Wisconsin schools has failed to keep pace with inflation. The latest school funding data arrived from DPI under the header: “Nearly two-thirds of districts will receive less aid due to flat state funding, antiquated funding formula,” 
About an hour later, a press release from Gov. Tony Evers’ office cheerfully announced that Wisconsin has ended the fiscal year with a $3.3 billion budget balance and a record  $2.1 billion in the state’s “rainy day” fund. The top line from the governor’s office message was upbeat: “Despite continued national economic turbulence, Wisconsin maintains strong fiscal position, reaching seven consecutive years of record-high General Fund balances during Gov. Evers’ tenure.”
These two announcements, although dramatically different in mood, are directly connected. The reason Wisconsin has a big budget surplus is largely because the state has abandoned its commitment to fund its public schools. 
A slide presentation by Anne Chapman, research director for the Wisconsin Association of School Business Officials graphically illustrates the decline in per-pupil spending on Wisconsin public school students since the 2008-2009 school year. Using Legislative Fiscal Bureau data, Chapman shows the steadily widening gap between the money schools would have had each year if revenue had kept pace with inflation and what they actually had. This year the shortfall reached $3,571 per kid. 
At the same time, schools have been carrying about $1.29 billion in special education costs that used to be paid for by the state. 
Schools have never bounced back from the drastic cuts to education spending during the administration of former Gov. Scott Walker. But the current budget situation is unprecedented, Chapman says. 
“The 2025-27 state budget provided no increase to general school aids. This was an extremely unusual policy choice, especially in light of the fact that the state had a $4.3 billion surplus going into the budget process,” she says. “The last instance of flat or negative general aids across both years of a biennial budget was the 2009-11 budget, at which time the state was facing a deficit.”
In other words, in a historic act of stinginess, the Legislature, while staring at a sizeable budget surplus, chose not to put a dime of it into public schools. That was a deliberate policy choice, not some sort of emergency measure taken under duress. 
Wisconsin’s school funding formula is complicated —  a mix of state and local funds divvied up based on school districts’ property wealth, enrollment numbers and spending patterns. Enrollment is figured out on a three-year rolling average, and different districts get different amounts of funding from the state — and some get none at all. When funding is flat, statewide, some districts get more and some get less. This is the “antiquated” system DPI referred to in its press release. It uses outdated metrics, and doesn’t account for the effects of high poverty or large numbers of English language learners. 
State schools superintendent Jill Underly expanded on this in her State of Education speech in September: “The formula places value on the wrong things. It values enrollment, district spending, and property value, rather than student needs. It fails to ask the most essential question: how much does it actually cost to educate the students who live in a district so that they have an equal opportunity to succeed? A student’s opportunity for success should not depend on their zip code. If we are going to improve the academic outcomes for ALL students, then the funding formula must prioritize student need.”
Because of the complexity of school finance, and the patchwork of have and have-not districts, it’s hard to figure the exact amount Wisconsin has underfunded its schools since 2009, when overall per-pupil spending stopped keeping pace with inflation. But you can get a rough, back of the envelope estimate by taking DPI’s total enrollment number from 2025-26  — 781,367 students — and multiplying it by the Legislative Fiscal Bureau’s estimate of the shortfall in per-pupil spending that year compared with inflation, which was $3,468.60. The number you get is $2.7 billion in combined state aid and property tax levies. If the state returned to its much-discussed commitment to fund two-thirds of the cost of public schools, that would mean we’d have to allocate $1.8 billion of the current $3.3 billion surplus to make schools whole. Add to that the $1.29 billion in special ed costs the state has sloughed off on the schools, and it reaches $3 billion.
One of the main effects of the state deciding not to fund schools is that the burden has fallen instead on local property taxpayers, who are confronting another surge in referendum requests from their local school districts in the voting booth this fall.   
Gov. Evers has proposed, by his own estimate in an address to the Wisconsin Public Education Network, $7 billion in new funding for schools that was rejected by the state Legislature over his two terms. He was bitterly disappointed when the state Senate rejected a $1.8 billion deal he struck with Republican legislative leaders that included some money for increased special education funding and property tax relief along with income tax cuts. 
But in his latest message, the governor embraces the unspent money sitting in state coffers as “damn good news.” 
“We’ve ended every fiscal year I’ve been governor with a positive balance,” he says. “We’ve shown that state government can work, and work better for the people we serve, and I’m incredibly proud of our efforts.”
Along with the surplus, the governor’s office celebrates the “largest balance in the ‘rainy day’ fund in state history” — at $2.1 billion, it’s  six times larger than when Evers took office.
Meanwhile, schools are in worse and worse shape, and all over the state, people are struggling to keep up with the cost of housing as property taxes rise. 
Whatever feeling of satisfaction there is in knowing the state has squirreled away a fat rainy day fund, when you look outside, it’s raining.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Another lawsuit filed over 2025 property tax legislation
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Three current and former legislators have filed another lawsuit over Senate Bill 542, a property tax bill signed last year.
State Sen. Greg Hertz, Senate Majority Leader Tom McGillvray and former legislator Keith Regier, all Republicans, jointly filed the lawsuit this week saying SB 542 violates the constitution’s equal protection clause. 
Under SB 542, residential property tax rates differ depending on their market value. The lawsuit, which was filed in Gallatin County, says setting different rates within the same property class violates the constitution.
“Tax relief for one group of Montanans should not come at the expense of unfairly taxing their neighbors. The Montana Constitution protects equal treatment, and we are asking the courts to enforce those protections,” McGillvray said in a press release. “This lawsuit is not about opposing property tax relief. It is about ensuring that tax relief is provided in a manner that respects the constitutional rights of every Montana property owner.”
The lawsuit says equal protection clauses protect individuals from “state action which selects him or her out for discriminatory treatment by subjecting him or her to taxes not imposed on others of the same class.”
Hertz, McGillvray and Regier previously filed a suit over the bill, saying it violated the constitution’s single-subject rule, which says a bill must address just one topic, and it must be clear. That suit, which the state GOP joined on the side of the plaintiffs, is still pending and was also filed in Gallatin County District Court.
“Montanans deserve a property tax system that is fair, transparent, and constitutional,” Hertz said in a press release. “The Legislature has the authority to establish property classifications, but once property is placed within the same class, the constitution requires that taxpayers be treated equally.”
SB 542 was passed during the 2025 session and signed into law by Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte. Some legislators referred to it as a “Frankstein” bill during the sessions, as it drew heavily from other legislation that didn’t pass.
The Governor’s Office did not immediately comment on the suit, but has expressed support for the legislation, saying 80% of Montanans got property tax relief.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators say Laurel could be breaking federal law
text:
Signs line the lawn of the Laurel Public Library as community resident gather before a listening session on a proposed state psychiatric facility. The meeting happened on April 22, 2026 (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). Montana legislators accused the City of Laurel of potentially breaking federal law in a fight over a mental health facility outside of the city in a meeting and a letter to the local government earlier this month.
Legislators in the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee also threatened to withhold municipal funding following a moratorium Laurel unanimously passed last month that halted annexing any land so it can study the city’s water system. Those issues also include aging infrastructure, fire protection problems and areas of low water pressure. There’s also been problems with the city’s water intake from the Yellowstone River.
State plans call for building a 32-bed mental health facility at the edge of Laurel city limits in Yellowstone County. Laurel residents have pushed back on the proposal citing problems they say could arise when the facility is built, including concerns the city’s utilities won’t be able to keep up.
City officials say they pressed pause on annexation applications so Laurel can study its water system. Some legislators, meanwhile, say the city is discriminating against those with mental illnesses and could be breaking federal law.  
A letter sent from the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee to Laurel and Montana’s congressional delegation says the city’s decision “essentially means the city will not provide water service to the proposed new mental health facility for forensic patients” and goes on to say the ordinance was “discriminatory.” 
State officials decided during the summer to place the facility outside Laurel. Onsite work at the facility has been paused while a lawsuit over the construction proceeds.
The letter from legislators to the City of Laurel says the action “may subject” the city to a lawsuit for violating federal law. Legislators unanimously approved the letter during an Oct. 8 committee meeting. 
Additionally, during that meeting, legislators by a 4-3 vote approved a “global motion” to direct the legislature to consider not directing any funding to any municipality under investigation for violations to the Americans with Disability Act, the Fair Housing Act or the Montana Human Rights Act.
The vote does not immediately strip any municipalities of any funding but means the issue of whether cities under federal investigation are eligible for state money will be taken up by the Legislative Finance Committee when it resumes during the 2027 session. Laurel was the only city discussed during the meeting.
“The legislature is not going to investigate the city of Laurel,” said John Esp, a Big Timber Republican and chairperson of the committee. “Somebody’s going to file a complaint on fair housing grounds, or on Americans with Disabilities grounds, or with the Montana Human Rights Commission, and while they’re under investigation by the Human Rights Commission or some federal agency, that’s when the prohibition on getting state money kicks in.”
Any sort of penalties wouldn’t begin unless the Legislature passes a bill to that effect next session.
When asked if any complaints have been filed against the City of Laurel, a Department of Labor and Industries employee within the Montana Human Rights Bureau directed the Daily Montanan to file a records request, which it has done. Federal Fair Housing Act violations would fall within the  U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, while Americans with Disabilities Act violations are investigated by a variety of federal entities.
In a five-page response to the lawmaker’s letter, Laurel Mayor Kris Vogele said he disagrees with the legislators, and expressed concern about any potential loss of funding. Some legislators worried the motion could negatively impact cities that are under investigation but end up not having broken federal law. Laurel receives millions of dollars in state funding per year, though city officials said they weren’t sure how much. 
For example, per the Montana League of Cities and Towns documentation, cities are projected to receive about $26 million in roads funding from the state, which is protected by statute. Laurel is projected to receive about $300,000 from that funding stream.
The legislative motion made by Sen. Ellie Boldman, a Missoula Democrat, said “that the legislature not consider or fund any local government request while under investigation for discriminating against a state facility.”
“Our intent right here on this call is to encourage the City of Laurel to take a look at this on their own,” Boldman said during the meeting, “so that nobody has to withhold anything.”
In a separate email to media members, Vogele said the committee was advancing a “deeply troubling allegation.”
“These are extraordinarily serious accusations, made with potentially far-reaching consequences not only for Laurel, but for communities across Montana,” Vogele wrote in a statement. “An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing. An allegation is not proof of discrimination. And a Montana community should not risk losing state funding simply because its elected officials raise legitimate questions about whether its infrastructure can safely support a major state project.”
The Laurel response also references a 95-page document the city sent the state regarding its environmental assessment of the mental health facility property. That document, sent to the state in September, asks for more assessment of the site “to establish a complete and supportable record.” 
The mental health facility has been an issue in Laurel for more than a year, and some residents have also expressed worry about the impacts to the city’s sewer and water systems, while others have been concerned about its location within a mile of an elementary school.

name: California
title: California’s ballot propositions fuel its longstanding tax-and-spending war
text:
California voters will pass judgment on 14 statewide ballot measures this year and all but two of them relate, in some manner, to financing public services.
Collectively they represent the latest version of what fiscal policy buffs call “ballot box budgeting” — persuading voters to prioritize or limit how funds are raised and spent rather than leaving those issues to elected officials.
This election’s most contentious measure, Proposition 40, typifies the underlying philosophical conflict that has raged ever since voters passed Proposition 13, the state’s iconic limit on property taxes, nearly a half-century ago.
Prop. 13 embodied the belief that high taxes undercut Californians’ ability to enhance the welfare of their own families. Prop. 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California’s billionaires, reflects the counter-contention that expansive public services better serve the well-being of all Californians.
Before Prop. 13 made the June 1978 ballot, the initiative process almost never dealt with tax and spending issues, a yearly summary from the secretary of state’s office indicates. Implicitly, voters were content to leave such money matters to elected state and local officials.
Prop. 13 reduced property taxes that had been the fundamental revenue source for local governments and school systems. It also made raising taxes of all kinds more difficult.
Prop. 13’s jolting impact also encouraged the use of ballot measures process not only to affect public finance issues but policies of all kinds. Succeeding elections saw an explosion of proposals dealing with such issues as punishment for crimes, immigration, affirmative action and same-sex marriage.
The two measures on this year’s ballot that don’t deal with taxes and spending typify that trend. Proposition 39 would require voters to show identifying documents and Proposition 45 would reduce use of the California Environmental Quality Act to block projects.
However, taxes and spending continued to dominate post-Prop. 13 elections, beginning in 1979 with a special election called by then-Gov. Jerry Brown to pass Proposition 4, a cap on state spending known as the “Gann Limit” for Paul Gann, a co-author of Prop. 13 with fellow tax gadfly Howard Jarvis.
Brown had strenuously opposed Prop. 13 but after its passage declared himself to be a “born-again tax cutter” and joined with Gann to persuade voters to approve the spending limit. It continues to be a factor in fashioning an annual state budget.
A much bigger budget factor is Proposition 98, a 1988 measure sponsored by the California Teachers Association to cushion Prop. 13’s impact on school finances. Prop. 98 contains a complex formula to guarantee a certain level of state education aid that works out to about 40% of general fund revenues.
The teachers’ union is opposing this year’s Prop. 40, the wealth tax on billionaires, which designates all but a small percentage of its revenue for healthcare, excluding Prop. 98. The conflict illustrates how ballot box budgeting pits interest groups against each other, even those on the same side in their underlying battle with anti-tax forces.
Speaking of which, anti-tax groups such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association have continued to press their cause, staving off efforts to change Prop. 13 and promoting tax limits.
This year, they are pushing Proposition 43, which would increase the vote requirement to approve some local taxes. And they’re opposing the California Teachers Association’s Proposition 3, which would make permanent a temporary tax on high-income Californians that was initially passed in 2012 at Brown’s behest during his second stint as governor.
During the 17th century, a conflict known as the 30 Years War raged in Europe. Today California’s war over taxes and spending is already 48 years old and, as this year’s array of ballot measures indicates, it shows no sign of ending.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Increases in farm building assessments fuel calls to revisit Indiana’s property valuation system
text:
A wind turbine near a rural Indiana farm in September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana farmers facing steep increases in building assessments are calling for changes to the state’s property valuation system, warning lawmakers Wednesday that similar structures are being assessed differently across county lines.
Indiana Farm Bureau representatives told the Interim Study Committee on Fiscal Policy that updated state cost tables have pushed up the assessed values of barns, grain bins and livestock facilities ahead of next year’s tax bills.
They urged lawmakers to address those discrepancies rather than leave individual property owners to challenge their assessments.
State officials acknowledged the concerns but cautioned that assessment changes alone would not resolve complaints about rising tax bills. They instead recommended preserving annual adjustments while improving assessment data and testing automated valuation tools.
Lawmakers also raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments climb as new or renovated houses change the surrounding market, and questioned whether new technology could help catch errors before taxpayers have to appeal.
The committee additionally heard an update on Indiana’s childcare voucher programs and proposals to finance expanded access ahead of the 2027 budget session. Discussions focused on sustaining the state’s recent voucher expansion and drawing more investment from employers, philanthropy and local governments.
Farm building increases draw concerns
Katrina Hall, Indiana Farm Bureau’s senior director of policy strategy and advocacy, said the organization commissioned Policy Analytics to examine agricultural building assessments after members began reporting large increases earlier this year.
The analysis initially showed a statewide increase of about 44% in assessed value for the agricultural buildings studied, she said. Later data, reflecting appeals and discussions with assessors, reduced that increase to 29% — still about $2 billion in additional assessed value for taxes payable in 2027.
More than half of the parcels in the later analysis had increases of at least 15%, Hall said. The figures show how much assessed values increased, not how much farmers’ tax bills will rise.
Story continues below.
attachment_6377
 
Hall said the discrepancies suggest a problem with statewide consistency. Some assessors made adjustments to the cost tables, she said, while others appeared to use them without similar changes. Identical buildings of the same age can consequently receive different values in neighboring counties.
She argued that appeals cannot substitute for correcting the underlying assessment process.
“Appeals are like a parcel at a time,” Hall said. “They are not fixing problems with assessing in the tax base.”
Farm Bureau wants the state to consider a nationally recognized valuation system, like Marshall & Swift, and examine outdated depreciation schedules. Hall said taxpayers seeking to challenge assessments often get appraisals using that system, creating a mismatch with the state’s tools.
The organization also proposed moving agricultural improvements from the 3% property tax cap category to the 2% category. Hall said its analysis estimated about $44 million in savings across agricultural properties.
That would be a tax relief change separate from revisions to assessment methods.
The proposals follow Indiana’s 2025 property tax overhaul, which changed homeowner deductions and credits, business personal property taxation and local government revenue rules.
A subsequent Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute analysis found that most homeowners would likely receive relief, but owners of low-value homes could face increases while more expensive homes received larger breaks.
State defends annual adjustments
Tim Rushenberg, general counsel for the Department of Local Government Finance, said Indiana can change its assessment tools, but the results must still meet constitutional requirements for uniform, equal and just valuations.
The department’s report explains that assessed value is only one part of a property tax bill, which also depends on local budgets, tax levies, deductions, credits and caps.
“An individual parcel can see a higher bill even when the district rate falls, or a lower bill despite increasing gross assessed value,” Rushenberg said. “There’s a lot of moving parts, so there is no reliable shortcut from gross assessed value to taxpayer impact.”
Annual adjustments, commonly called trending, help keep assessments aligned with market evidence between physical reassessments, he said.
Story continues below.
attachment_6376
 
Less frequent updates could reduce annual changes but allow inequities to accumulate and produce larger increases when properties are eventually reassessed. Limits tied to purchase prices or annual assessment growth could also raise constitutional questions if comparable properties receive different treatment.
Cost tables provide a common starting point for estimating property values, Rushenberg continued, but their results must remain open to challenge using credible evidence.
Barry Wood, the department’s assessment division director, said the state previously updated cost schedules once every four years. It’s moving toward annual review of the schedules or a related adjustment factor to help limit large fluctuations.
Rushenberg said the department wants construction costs, appraisals and other evidence to evaluate whether particular agricultural building schedules need correction. Public comments on readoption of the state’s real property assessment rule close Oct. 23.
“We want to look at the data,” Rushenberg said. “We’ve asked for data to see where, maybe in the cost schedule, something isn’t adding up there. But we certainly don’t want to make a general assumption that an entire schedule is is incorrect.”
Homeowners face hurdles, too
Rep. Cherrish Pryor, D-Indianapolis, raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments rise as new or renovated houses elevate housing prices, even when they have made no improvements themselves.
She urged officials to make the process easier to understand and reduce the need for homeowners to challenge inaccurate values.
“We live it, and so it’s easy for us, but it’s not easy for the average person, particularly if you’re an older individual,” Pryor said.
Wood said assessors can distinguish between different types and ages of homes within a neighborhood when applying adjustments.



Quotation







Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences.


– Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis


Automated valuation models could help identify inconsistencies requiring closer review, said Hamilton County Assessor Kevin Poore. An assessor-led pilot is underway in Hendricks, Clark, Lake, Vanderburgh, LaPorte and Allen counties.
The department recommended beginning with an advisory or quality-control pilot, retaining local assessor judgment and taxpayers’ notice and appeal rights.
Still, Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis, pressed for clear error measures and analysis of who would pay more or less before broader implementation.
“Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences,” Qaddoura said.
Childcare funding debate continues
Also Wednesday, Adam Alson, director of the Office of Early Childhood and Out-of-School Learning, said Gov. Mike Braun intends to continue the voucher expansion supported by a one-time $200 million infusion announced this spring.
“The additional 14,000 CCDF vouchers are funded solely with state dollars and for one fiscal year,” Alson said. “The governor is committed to continuing this increase in enrollment, and as such, this additional investment and allocation will be reflected in its upcoming budget.”
September figures presented to the committee showed 46,579 children enrolled across the Child Care and Development Fund and On My Way Pre-K programs, with 17,732 on their combined waitlists.

Regulated childcare capacity nevertheless fell about 3.3% from a year earlier, to 156,151 seats.
Alson said the administration is pursuing regulatory changes and additional ways for employers, philanthropy and local governments to invest.
Whitney Coake, a Taft public affairs director speaking on her own behalf, proposed a “QuadShare” framework combining employer, taxpayer, state and philanthropic contributions. It would fund expanded childcare assistance, 12 weeks of paid parental leave and an early care trust fund.
Her model estimated about $1.74 billion in annual operating expenses, separate from proposed trust fund deposits. Financing would include a 0.3% employer payroll contribution and a 0.15 percentage-point increase in the individual income tax rate. Philanthropic contributions and investment returns remain proposed or illustrative.
Alson emphasized that communities need flexibility to develop approaches suited to their families and employers.
“There are places throughout the state that are saying this is important,” he said. “How do we figure out how we do it?”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand, Lahn debate plans to tackle state budget shortfall while funding schools
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, and businessman Zach Lahn, a Republican, are competing to become Iowa governor in the 2026 election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Iowa gubernatorial candidates Rob Sand and Zach Lahn contrasted their proposals Wednesday during a televised debate on how to fund Iowa priorities amid both a state budget deficit and high inflation rate.
The debate, hosted by KTIV-TV4 in Sioux City, was the second time the candidates met on stage as they seek to fill the seat held by Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who is not seeking reelection in 2026.
Lahn and Sand spent less time focused on countering campaign ad attacks than during their first debate with KWQC, held at St. Ambrose University in Davenport, when Lahn, a Republican businessman who owns a farm in Belle Plaine, said his opponent was attacking his family and children by bringing his Iowa residency into question in campaign rhetoric.
At this debate, Lahn and Sand said they respected one another for their work as fathers and as people willing to take on the task of campaigning for Iowa governor. They also spent more time sharing their ideas, concerns and policy proposals on issues like education and taxes if elected.
Sand, a Democrat, repeated a pledge he made in the campaign to provide a 5% State Supplemental Aid rate increase for a K-12 funding in his first year in office. But he also sad he has told supporters and education activists that he “can’t promise that in year two.”
What to know as early voting begins in Iowa for 2026 general election

Sand said he could not make a promise for further increased funding in light of the state’s budget deficit. The Iowa Revenue Estimating Conference said in March that state revenues are expected to decrease by 9.3% from fiscal years 2025 to 2026, a greater drop than previously predicted. Republicans leaders, in control of both chambers in the Iowa Legislature, and Reynolds have said these revenue decreases were expected after changes were made to the state’s income tax system, but predicted that increased revenues through sales and use taxes, as well personal income taxes will offset the deficit in future years.
Sand was skeptical of this view of Iowa Republicans’ tax plan. He said he believed it was vital to provide a 5% increase to K-12 school funding in his first year in office, but being able to invest in the future — and in other programs he supports like “free school lunch,” would require the state to address the budget deficit and find new streams of revenue.
“We have to see where we’re going with the state’s budget,” Sand said. “That deficit, we’ve got to do something to address it. But, we could do that 5% increase, and if we are taking away tax deals for data centers, if we legalize cannabis, treat it like alcohol — the first year will probably see $50 million, but in years after that, we’ll be over $100 million.”
Lahn presented a different opinion on education funding. He said the State Board of Education should be given the ability to create “innovation zones” across the state, which he said would “give teachers and superintendents more opportunity to be able to teach in different ways to meet the needs of more students.”
“If you want to see what’s happening, just look at the rate at which teachers are leaving the profession in year one, two, or three,” Lahn said. “It’s just unacceptable. They want to help the next generation. So through innovative practices, we could actually create school choice within our public schools. We’ll have concurrent models of school that parents can opt into a more innovative method — not an experiment, something that’s been happening across the country for decades, oftentimes. That is an area that we really can focus in to increased funding.”
He also said “cultural issues” present a large problem for school teachers, who he said were being treated as behavioral specialists for some students.
“There’s 95% of their time is largely spent with 5% of the kids,” Lahn said. “And these are kids who, you know, from my own experience, having spent so many hours working with children, these are kids that are crying out for help. They’re looking for somebody to help them, even if they don’t know it. … We need to be the first state in the country to create non-punitive off ramps for these kids, to get them the one-on-one and small group help that they need.”
When the moderator asked if education spending increases must exceed the current national inflation rate of 3.7%, Lahn said the question was “not exactly the best governance question,” because work would need to be done to calculate how best to “bring more innovation into our classrooms.” He also said he did not believe measuring this cost against inflation was an effective way to ensure Iowa students are receiving the best education possible.
He pointed to phonics-based reading programs, a reversal from other reading curricula that taught students to identify and learn words using contextual clues, as an example of a way to improve Iowa schools without needing to put further money in the K-12 system.
“Making those changes really doesn’t cost us a whole lot more money at all to improve our rankings,” Lahn said. “There’s things that we can do that are very cost-effective to improve rankings. This is something I’m most excited about, is to work with our public schools to do that.”
Lahn also has called for fully eliminating the state’s personal income tax — and said he was interested in, over the long term, eliminating property taxes on primary resident, single-family homes. While Lahn has stated he would work to find inefficiencies that could reduce government spending to offset the loss in revenue from the tax, he also said there are other areas where revenue can be generated. He pointed to removing tax breaks for data centers — a proposal Sand also supports — and making more information on government spending publicly accessible online for Iowans to check and find inconsistencies.
“But I have heard people talk about, I think it’s a two-and-a-half cent increase in the sales tax would cover almost the entire burden of single family primary residences in the state,” Lahn said. “That is not my proposal, but it’s one option I’ve heard people float.”
Moderators added some levity into the debate by asking the candidates about personal preferences. Sand told the hosts his favorite flavor of pie was strawberry rhubarb while Lahn’s was Oreo cream pie. Both said pizza was their favorite school lunch.
Sand and Lahn will debate for a third and final time on “Iowa Press” Wednesday, Oct. 21.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG finds ‘substantial share’ of Project Jupiter public comments raise concerns
text:
A rendering of Project Jupiter with a public comment in which an Albuquerque resident writes that prior comments in favor of the development made under her name were submitted without her knowledge or consent. (Rendering courtesy of STACK Infrastructure)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a Wednesday letter to New Mexico Environment Department Secretary James Kenney said that a “substantial share” of public comments on the pending air quality permit application for the Project Jupiter data center were “not sent by members of the public acting on their own.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Source NM in June revealed how residents in New Mexico’s three largest cities said their names falsely appeared on pro-Project Jupiter comments after they were approached by canvassers representing the Oracle and OpenAI data center. Several elected officials — in the state Legislature and on city councils across the state — subsequently said their names were similarly misused, prompting Torrez to open an investigation.
Torrez’s Wednesday letter to Kenney said the New Mexico Department of Justice’s review is “ongoing.”
“As it proceeds, we will evaluate whether the conduct described in this letter may also violate New Mexico criminal laws, and we will expand the inquiry accordingly,” Torrez wrote.
In his letter, Torrez said his office analyzed all 17,419 comments submitted during the public comment period for the data center’s air quality permit application.
If approved, the air quality permit would enable developers to use a natural-gas powered fuel cell system to power Project Jupiter. Projections show it could emit as many greenhouse gases annually as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
Torrez said that about 60% of the public comments — between 10,000 and 10,600 — contained the same pro-Project Jupiter form letter and came from 9,000 internet addresses, most of which submitted one comment apiece. Most listed out-of-state phone numbers even though the public comment portal didn’t require a portal, Torrez said.
He added that many of the form letters matched the supporter list associated with Project Jupiter’s website, projectjupitertogether.com, which hosts an interactive form letter titled “Send a comment to NMED.”
About 4,700 comments, most of which opposed the permit application, came from just 17 internet addresses, Torrez said.
Torrez wrote that he wanted “to be precise about the limits of what we know.”
“This letter does not establish who is responsible for any particular comment, and it does not characterize anyone’s intent,” he continued. “It does establish that a number of comments cannot be read as a measure of public opinion until the record has been verified.”
The NMDOJ review also turned up 22 comments bearing the names of public officials, local governments and organizations that all came from one computer, Torrez wrote, adding that “several of the officials named in those filings have informed my office that they did not write or authorize the submissions made in their names.”
“Taken together, these patterns mean that a substantial share of the comments was not sent by members of the public acting on their own,” he wrote.
Torrez asked NMED to preserve records including IP addresses and submission timestamps, to set aside the comments he’s flagged and to mark them as unverified. He also asked NMED officials to seek a ruling from the hearing officer presiding over the air quality permit application as to whether the flagged comments should be “considered in determining significant public interest.”
If the records can’t be verified, Torrez advised NMED to consider reopening its public comment period.
Torrez added that his office is asking Project Jupiter’s developers, its consultants and vendors to preserve corresponding records.
In a statement to Source NM, NMED spokesperson Drew Goretzka said that Kenney and Torrez met Wednesday morning to discuss the ongoing investigation.
“Secretary Kenney appreciates Attorney General Torrez’s investigation of this matter, and the New Mexico Environment Department will continue to preserve records in support of the New Mexico Department of Justice’s investigation,” Goretzka said. “While NMED has strengthened security measures in its public comment system, any person or organization that attempts to misuse the public comment process to steer a permit decision should be held accountable. NMED looks forward to continuing to work with the NMDOJ as the investigation proceeds, including helping in any resulting civil or criminal proceedings, as appropriate.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: AccelerateMS seeks $2.5M budget increase to expand staff and workforce programs
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s workforce development agency is seeking more state money to add staff as it launches and expands job training programs. The request comes as the state prepares for thousands of jobs to open in the next decade. 
AccelerateMS is requesting a $7.1 million operating budget for fiscal year 2028, which begins July 1. That is about $2.5 million more than its current appropriation, according to information that agency officials recently presented to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee. The increase would go toward hiring staff to help manage new programs, including UPSKILL (Upgrading Priority Skills for Key Industry Learning and Labor), which launched this summer, and the new Workforce Pell Grant program, said Courtney Taylor, executive director of AccelerateMS. 
The State Workforce Investment Board estimated in 2025 that Mississippi will face a shortage of 19,000 workers in priority fields such as manufacturing, construction and healthcare through 2035. Taylor said closing the gap will require the state to train more workers and students and to connect them to high-demand jobs. 
“The investment is crucial for our state and to meet the economy where it’s going,” Taylor said. 
AccelerateMS currently has 28 employees, Taylor said, and wants to hire an additional eight. 
One of those positions is a full-time Workforce Pell manager, Taylor said. The  Workforce Pell Grant program launched in July will allow eligible students to use federal Pell Grants for certain short-term job training programs. 
The expansion of the Pell Grant program, which traditionally helped low-income students pay for college, will allow students to pay for workforce programs lasting as little as eight to 15 weeks. 
Having a dedicated employee to review applications from the state’s universities, community and technical colleges seeking approval for eligible programs to qualify for Workforce Pell would help, she said. For now, an employee who oversees other federal initiatives, including the opioid-settlement workforce training program, reviews Workforce Pell applications. 
In September, Mississippi secured $8.5 million in federal funding to help launch Workforce Pell across all 15 community colleges.
Northwest Mississippi Community College will lead the effort, but AccelerateMS will help to coordinate and set up the program statewide, Taylor said. 
Workforce Pell requires a lot of management, including tracking data required by the federal government for students’ graduation rates, job placement and wage outcomes, said Iris Palmer, director of community college initiatives at New America, a national public policy think tank. 
The requirements for Workforce Pell “are very complicated,” and the process of getting these types of programs set up at colleges can be difficult, she said.  
Lawmakers will consider AccelerateMS’s request during their three-month session that begins in January, as they finalize the state budget for the next fiscal year. 
State Sen. Briggs Hopson III, R-Vicksburg, answers questions from fellow senators during a special session at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Wednesday, May 28, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Senate Appropriations Chairman Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg, said it is too early to know whether AccelerateMS will receive its full request. Lawmakers are reviewing agencies’ budget requests and the state’s major spending needs, including Medicaid, he said. Hopson said lawmakers will consider how much money the state has available and determine where it can be spent when developing the final budget.
